images.prompt: Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama. A round countdown dial about the size of a saucer stands on a brushed graphite base at the left of a pale neutral tabletop. Its front is sandblasted frosted glass divided into seven wedge segments around a plain centre, all softly lit from within. To the right lies a single project folder of heavy ivory card, closed, with a crisp spine and an unmarked tab, and an acid-lime elastic band stretched once around it, still sealed. Behind, a graphite in-tray holds two loose task cards. A graphite pen rests parallel to the folder, and a frosted mug waits nearby, full. Fine dust edges the dial's segment lines, and the folder's card shows long parallel fibres. Wide 16:9 landscape frame. The hero object sits slightly left of centre on the lower third, with the related objects extending to the right so the workflow reads left to right. Clean, generous negative space above. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: one large soft key light from the upper left at about 45 degrees, like diffused north-window daylight, with a gentle white bounce fill from the right; soft grounded contact shadows fall to the lower right. Camera: 100mm macro lens at f/4, eye level with the tabletop, three-quarter view. The hero object is tack sharp and the background melts into smooth, creamy blur on a seamless pale neutral sweep. Mood: calm, precise, orderly and quietly premium, like high-end editorial product photography. Strictly no people, figures, faces, hands or silhouettes. No readable text, letters, numbers, clock digits, logos, signage or user-interface graphics anywhere. No holograms, floating screens, robots with faces, dense cable tangles, carnival or circus elements, cartoon or plastic CGI look, oversaturated colour, lens flare or heavy vignette.

Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama, captured mid-disaster. The same dial, running down. Four of the seven frosted segments have gone dark grey, a fifth is dimming, and the last two glow faintly. The project folder still lies closed, its acid-lime elastic band untouched, but work has piled up around it: task cards have spilled from the in-tray and banked against the folder in slanting drifts, some caught sliding over its top. The pen has vanished under cards. The mug sits cold with a skin on its surface and has been shoved to the edge by the advancing drift. Loose cards flutter off the right side. A thin dust hangs in front of the dimming segments, and the drift slopes back toward the tray. Wide 16:9 landscape frame, same layout and angle as the calm version of this scene. The hero object stays slightly left of centre, and the spread of the disaster runs to the right and toward the camera so its path can be traced back to the source. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: the same soft upper-left key and right-side bounce fill as a calm studio setup, unchanged, so the disorder reads as physical and real rather than theatrical. Airborne paper, grains and fragments catch the key light with crisp edge highlights. Camera: 85mm lens at f/5.6, same three-quarter tabletop angle, fast shutter freezing everything mid-air. Focus sits where the chain reaction started, and the spread softens into the depth of field. Mood: absurd but plausible, an orderly system that got out of hand, still clean and editorial. Photorealistic photograph of a vast handcrafted miniature landscape diorama. A deep, terraced quarry drops away below the viewer, its stepped walls built from thousands of compressed ivory folders, spines bleached, curled and split, descending in broad benches toward a shadowed floor. Beyond the far rim, a pale plain runs to a hazy horizon. On the near rim, the giant countdown dial lies cracked and fully dark, half sunk in a drift of task cards. On the quarry floor, the original project folder sits closed, pinned under loose cards. A slim graphite derrick braced on the rim lowers a lime lifting line straight down, its graphite hook clasped around the folder's spine, and the folder is just beginning to rise, shedding a trickle of cards. Wide 16:9 panoramic frame. The main ruin anchors the left or centre foreground, terrain rolls back to a distant horizon on the upper third, and the lime recovery rig sits in the right midground. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: soft overcast late-afternoon daylight still falling from the upper left, with long soft shadows grounding the ruins and atmospheric haze fading distant forms into pale grey-green. Camera: wide 24mm view from a low vantage just above the terrain, deep focus through the midground, with a gentle tilt-shift falloff at the top and bottom edges so the vast scene still reads as a miniature diorama. Mood: quiet, desolate and monumental, but hopeful at the lime recovery rig, which is the sharpest and brightest point of interest. Strictly no people, figures, faces, hands or silhouettes.
